value: in a field distance experiment, wild-caught settlement-stage Ambon damselfish showed no bite-rate difference between conspecific alarm odour and seawater at 0.1 and 0.5 m downcurrent of dead-degraded coral, but alarm odour-exposed fish reduced bite rate by 50% at 2 and 5 m
units: categorical (change in bite rate, post-cue minus pre-cue, by cue and distance downcurrent of degraded coral)
method: field behavioural assay on live-coral patch reefs (25 x 20 x 20 cm, Pocillopora damicornis) at four distances (0.1, 0.5, 2, 5 m) downcurrent of a natural bank of dead-degraded coral at the reef edge; each fish habituated 20 to 60 min, then 60 ml of cue injected through a 2 m tube up-current of the patch and flushed with 60 ml seawater; behaviour scored by an observer over 3 min before and 3 min after the cue; bite rate was one of four variables (also distance moved, distance ventured, boldness); 2 (cue: conspecific alarm odour versus seawater) x 4 (distance) ANOVA
conditions: wild-sourced: settlement-stage juveniles caught at night in light traps moored at least 30 m from the reef edge at Lizard Island (Great Barrier Reef), held in flow-through seawater tanks and used within 4 days of capture; experiments October to December 2016, 13 days spread over a month, two sites; each fish used once; 10 to 15 replicates per cue-by-distance cell (exact n per cell is in the Fig. 2 legend, not read); alarm odour made by macerating one recently settled conspecific juvenile (12 to 14 mm standard length) in about 100 ml seawater, no concentration stated; seawater cue controlled for introduction of an odour onto the patch; Cue x Distance interaction F3,94 = 11.03, p < 0.0001; same-section result: change in distance moved, distance ventured and boldness showed the same pattern as bite rate, with the reaction to alarm odour occurring only once at least 2 m from the bank of dead coral; separate laboratory experiment (not this value) found water over dead-degraded coral, Okeania sp. or Pseudo-nitzschia sp. gave no significant alarm response against seawater controls

source.authors: McCormick MI, Barry RP, Allan BJM
source.title: Algae associated with coral degradation affects risk assessment in coral reef fishes

quote: There was no difference in bite rate between cues at 0.1 and 0.5 m, but the bite rates of the alarm odour-exposed fish were reduced by 50% at 2 and 5 m from the source of the degraded water [...]
note: Classification: behavioural response (bite rate) of wild-caught juvenile fish to a conspecific skin-extract alarm odour in the field; no chemoreceptor is identified. The quote is the first half of one Results sentence, cut at the figure reference '(Fig. 2a)' (marked [...]); the omitted remainder reads 'suggesting that the efficacy of alarm odour to inform risk was restored due to increased distance from degraded coral' and is the authors' interpretation. The null at 0.1 and 0.5 m is part of the value; the paper attributes it to degraded-coral water masking the alarm odour, and the abstract says fish 'were not able to detect alarm odours within 2 m downcurrent of degraded coral' (reader-assembled). Design: the manipulated variable is distance from degraded coral, with the alarm-versus-seawater contrast within each distance; the response is a pre-to-post-cue difference. Fish were held in the laboratory up to 4 days before field release onto patches. value: in free-ranging field camera-trap tests of three attractants against a water control, cadaverine was the most effective attractant for wild Iberian wolves (Canis lupus signatus)
units: categorical (wolf detection at camera-trap sampling points by attractant; GLMM)
method: free-ranging field trial: a camera trap in front of each sampling point holding 5 ml of attractant (or water as control) on a stone; attractants cadaverine (the authors' own water solution of rotten fish, concentration not stated), Fatty Acid Scent (FAS, a mixture of ten synthetic volatile fatty acids) and lynx urine; sampling unit the day at a sampling point, a day positive if wolves were detected at least once from midnight to midnight; relative activity index and detection-probability GLMMs
conditions: wild-sourced: free-ranging wolves in Sierra de la Demanda (La Rioja, Spain); phase 1 over 125 days June to October 2022 with four sampling points and a sheep-leg bait with and without bait, two sampling zones, attractant restocked (5 ml) every 10 days; phase 2 for 28 days November to December 2022 with all attractants at four sampling points, two blocks 8 km apart, restocked every 7 days; sampling units n = 8 (reader-assembled); same-section results: only cadaverine had a significant effect on wolf detection (estimate 2.85 +/- 1.05 SE, Z = 2.7, p = 0.006) and significantly increased detection compared with control in post hoc tests (Z = 2.70, p = 0.03), whereas FAS and lynx urine did not differ significantly from the control; daily detection probabilities cadaverine 0.025, FAS 0.005, lynx urine 0.008; the unbaited control had no visits (RAI 0.00); including bait had no significant effect on wolf visitation rates (models with bait had higher AIC); the paper's separate captivity trial with six captive wolves is not part of this value

source.authors: Del Río L, Zearra JA, Mateo R, Ferreras P, Tobajas J
source.title: Effectiveness of attractants and bait for Iberian wolf detection: captivity-based and free-ranging trials

quote: Specifically, cadaverine was the most effective attractant for wild Iberian wolves.
note: Classification: behavioural response (detection at camera-trap scent stations) of free-ranging wolves to a food-decay odour; no chemoreceptor is identified and the detection is a visit, not a measured preference. The paper studies the Iberian wolf (Canis lupus signatus), and the Mammal Diversity Database page for Canis lupus Linnaeus 1758 (mammaldiversity.org/taxon/1005943, opened; it printed the name and authority, its status field blank, and did not mention signatus) is the authority page, so the record is logged at species level.
